pool.prompt: An OSP engineer is designing feeder plant for a GPON FTTH network. The OLT vendor specs state the optical budget is Class B+. What does this tell the OSP engineer?
choices: The OLT requires B+ rated fiber cable jackets in the conduit
The total optical loss from the OLT port to the subscriber ONT cannot exceed 28 dB — this budget must cover fiber loss, splitter loss, splice loss, and connector loss
The downstream transmission speed is limited to a B+ tier (100 Mb/s per subscriber)
The OLT can only serve subscribers within a Class B service area (within city limits)
pool.explanation: Class B+ is an ITU-T G.984.2 optical budget class specifying a maximum 28 dB loss from OLT port to ONT (13 dB minimum). This is the fundamental constraint on the OSP link budget: fiber attenuation + splitter loss + connector loss + splice loss + margin must all fit within 28 dB.
pool.citation: ITU-T G.984.2 — Gigabit-Capable Passive Optical Networks (GPON): Physical Media Dependent (PMD) Layer Specification.

pool.prompt: In a GPON network, which wavelength does the OLT use to transmit data to subscribers (downstream)?
choices: 850 nm
pool.explanation: GPON uses 1490 nm downstream (OLT to ONT) and 1310 nm upstream (ONT to OLT). Both signals travel on the same single fiber simultaneously — WDM (Wavelength Division Multiplexing) filters at each end separate the two wavelengths. An optional third wavelength (1550 nm) can carry a CATV video overlay.

pool.prompt: An OLT line card fails at the headend, taking down service for 200 subscribers. An OSP technician is asked to help troubleshoot. What should they check in the OSP plant?
choices: Nothing — the line card is inside-plant equipment. OSP plant has no role in a line card failure.
Check the feeder fiber OTDR trace for a break that may have caused the line card to fail due to high-power reflection
Verify which feeder fibers connect to the failed line card's ports (using the splice matrix), then trace those feeder runs for any OSP-side fault (break, macro-bend, water intrusion at a splice case)
Replace the OLT chassis with a backup unit
pool.explanation: Even though the failure looks like a line-card problem, the OSP technician should rule out an OSP-side fault. Use the splice matrix to identify which OSP feeder fibers connect to the failed line card's ports, then OTDR those feeders. An unrelated OSP plant issue (water intrusion, break) can cause OLT port events that get misdiagnosed as a line-card failure.
pool.citation: Field troubleshooting practice; consistent with ITU-T G.984.2 PON architecture.

pool.prompt: An ISP is planning a new FTTH build and tells the OSP engineer they plan to use XGS-PON (10 Gb/s symmetric). The OSP engineer has already designed the feeder plant using standard G.652.D OS2 fiber with 1:32 splitters. Does the OSP plant need to be redesigned?
choices: Yes — XGS-PON requires a completely different fiber type with lower attenuation
Yes — the splitter ratio must change from 1:32 to 1:8 because XGS-PON cannot support more than 8 subscribers per port
No — XGS-PON runs on the same G.652.D single-mode fiber with a similar optical budget class and split ratios. The OSP plant is compatible; the OLT equipment swap at the headend is sufficient.
No — but all connectors must be replaced with a different type before XGS-PON can be used
pool.explanation: XGS-PON (ITU-T G.9807.1) uses the same G.652.D OS2 single-mode fiber as GPON, with a similar optical budget class and split ratio range. Upgrading from GPON to XGS-PON is a headend equipment swap, not an outside-plant rebuild — one of the key long-term value propositions of a passive-fiber OSP architecture: the outside plant is generation-agnostic.

pool.prompt: What is the fundamental architectural difference between an OLT-driven GPON network and a CMTS-driven HFC (cable) network, from the OSP engineer's perspective?
choices: GPON has no OSP fiber component at all; HFC is fiber-only

In GPON, all splits between the OLT and the subscriber are passive (no powered electronics in the OSP feeder path); in HFC, the optical node is an active, powered device in the OSP plant that converts fiber to coax
GPON and HFC use identical passive splitter architectures — the only difference is the connector type
HFC networks do not require an OSP engineer at all because CMTS handles all distribution electronically
pool.explanation: GPON's split architecture is entirely passive — splitter cassettes in an FDH or pedestal, no active electronics between OLT and ONT. HFC's optical node is an active, powered device that must be powered in the OSP plant (via coax or a separate AC circuit) and converts fiber to RF coax. This distinction matters for OSP power planning on HFC builds.
pool.citation: Industry-standard PON vs. HFC architecture comparison.

pool.prompt: An OLT line card typically provides how many GPON ports?
choices: 1–2 ports
8–16 ports
64–128 ports
500+ ports
pool.explanation: OLT line cards typically provide 8–16 GPON ports. Actual port counts are vendor- and model-specific — always verify the OLT specification sheet for the equipment being deployed. Each port can serve up to 32 or 64 subscribers through passive splitters in the OSP plant.

pool.prompt: GPON specifies SC/APC connectors at the OLT optical interface. Why does GPON require APC (angled) rather than UPC (flat/ultra-polished) connectors?
choices: APC connectors are cheaper to manufacture at scale
APC's angled ferrule face (−65 dB reflectance) reduces back-reflection compared to UPC; high reflectance from a UPC connector degrades GPON upstream link performance
APC connectors have a larger core diameter, which is required for the higher power of GPON downstream signals
UPC connectors are physically incompatible with SC housings
pool.explanation: SC/APC's angled physical contact reduces back-reflection to roughly −65 dB, versus the much higher reflectance of a flat SC/UPC connector. In GPON, elevated back-reflection at any point in the optical path can degrade upstream link performance for the shared PON branch — this is why APC is the GPON standard.

pool.prompt: Match each element of the GPON signal path to whether it is OSP scope or ISP scope.

targets.label: OLT GPON port → ODF patch cord

pool.explanation: The OLT-to-ODF patch cord is inside-plant/ISP work. Everything from the ODF splice outward — the pigtail-to-feeder splice, the feeder fiber itself, and the FDH passive splitter — is OSP design and construction scope.
